newsitem.title: ZAIRE: East Zaire arabica coffee picking up after war.
newsitem.headline: East Zaire arabica coffee picking up after war.

text.p: Rebel-held eastern Zaire's arabica coffee region is recovering after months of insecurity but near-term quality and quantity will both suffer, dealers and growers say.

Plunged into war by the arrival of rebel troops in November, the prime arabica growing regions of North and South Kivu have suffered lingering security problems as the rebels have advanced deeper into Zaire.

"The plantation is overgrown and the workers have fled because of the insecurity, it may not be quite as bad on the small holdings but it will take everybody a while to recover," said one plantation supervisor in the eastern town of Goma.

Official figures for the annual arabica crop are highly variable, and distorted by smuggling into neighbouring Rwanda and Uganda. Before the war arabica exports were estimated at above 12,000 tonnes and up to 20,000 tonnes.
"The smaller crop from April to June will certainly be hit this year, both in terms of quality and quantity, although it is hard to really say by how much," said one local buyer.
The main crop harvest north of Goma begins in September.

Initial predictions that farmers would quickly be able to return to their fields proved over-optimistic as skirmishes continued on a local level between the rebels and both former village warrior allies and remnants of Rwandan Hutu militias.

"It may not be so much a problem for the smallholders, but the plantations were badly looted as well and right now there is just not the money to invest in starting things up again," the supervisor said.
However foreign buyers are showing increasing interest in Zaire at the main exporting points of Goma and Beni.
"We are looking possibly at lower prices here as well as more liberal rules under the new administration," said one Uganda-based buyer.
Customs officials said that apart from several hundred tonnes of coffee seized late last year by rebel soldiers, small amounts had been exported officially since January.

"We changed the rules to allow anybody who wants to export to come here, as long as they pay for the licence, although it still has to be milled here and exported under a Zairean label," said rebel finance commissioner Mawapanga Mwana Nanga.
Coffee is the most easily available export in the area under rebel control, and potentially an important source of revenue for the war to overthrow president of 31 years Mobutu Sese Seko.

The bulk of Zaire's crop is robusta, growing in the tropical basin of which only the extremities have fallen under rebel control, and exported via the Atlantic port of Matadi or smuggled to neighbouring countries.
Dealers in Goma said that exports from the robusta growing region of Upper Zaire, which is now held by the rebels, would be made difficult by poor road access from the east.
